fields.loses: mark type usually lost: M method, A accuracy, B independent
fields.groups: skill groups it applies to ('*' = any skill)

codes.definition: Rounds an intermediate value, so the final answer drifts outside the accuracy accepted.
Gives the final answer to the wrong number of decimal places or significant figures.
Gives a decimal when an exact answer (surd, fraction, pi, ln) was asked for.
Has the right value but not in the form the question specifies, e.g. constants not identified.
In a show-that, jumps to the printed answer without the step that justifies it.
Starts from the printed result, or uses it as if true, instead of deriving it.
Writes only a calculator answer where the question requires working, so method marks cannot be given.
Uses a fresh method when 'hence' requires the previous result.
Leaves out or misstates units on a contextual answer.
Makes a numerical slip in an otherwise correct method.
Loses a minus sign when expanding or removing brackets, especially -(a - b).
Copies a number or expression wrongly from the question or from earlier working.
Keeps a solution that is impossible in the context or domain, e.g. a negative length.
Throws away a solution that is actually valid.
Does the working but never states the answer or the conclusion the question asks for.
Gives a bare number where an interpretation in the context is needed.
Writes a solution set wrongly, e.g. an intersection sign where the regions are joined by 'or'.
Finds a different quantity from the one asked, e.g. x when the question wants y.
Gives a reason that does not name the specific feature or value the explanation depends on.
Uses a correct method on an earlier answer but then changes or ignores that earlier value, losing the follow-through.
Misapplies index laws, e.g. (x^a)^b as x^(a+b), or 1/sqrt(x) as x^(1/2).
Splits a fraction over a sum in the denominator: 1/(a + b) as 1/a + 1/b.
Cancels individual terms of a sum instead of common factors.
Undoes an operation wrongly when changing the subject, or applies it to only one term.
Multiplies by the wrong conjugate, or only multiplies the numerator, when rationalising a denominator.
Treats sqrt(a + b) as sqrt(a) + sqrt(b), or combines unlike surds.
Adds when it should subtract (or the reverse), or scales only part of an equation, when eliminating.
Finds one unknown or coordinate but not the matching second one.
Solving x^n = k for even n, keeps only the positive root.
Misremembers the quadratic formula, e.g. +b, or divides only the square root by 2a.
Factorises with the wrong signs, giving roots of the wrong sign.
Divides both sides by x or by a factor and loses the solution where it is zero.
Doesn't take out the x^2 coefficient first, halves wrongly, or gets the constant wrong.
Uses the wrong discriminant condition for the number of roots, e.g. > 0 for equal roots, or > for >=.
Reads a, b, c before rearranging the equation to equal zero.
Finds the critical values correctly, then chooses the region inside when it should be outside, or the reverse.
Multiplies or divides an inequality by a negative number without reversing the sign.
Solves for the substituted variable but never converts back, e.g. stops at e^x = 3 or keeps e^x = -2.
Evaluates f(a) for the factor (x + a) instead of f(-a).
Evaluates f at the root but never sets it equal to zero (or to the remainder).
Makes a subtraction sign error in long division, or leaves out a zero term.
Stops at a quadratic factor that still factorises.
Treats a touching root as a single root, or reads the sign of the leading coefficient wrongly from the graph.
Moves f(x + a) to the right instead of the left, or stretches f(ax) by a instead of 1/a.
Applies a combination of transformations in the wrong order.
Leaves out or misplaces the intercepts, turning points or asymptote values the sketch must show.
Draws the wrong shape: crosses an asymptote, wrong end behaviour, or a cusp where the curve is smooth.
Confuses y = |f(x)| with y = f(|x|), reflecting the wrong part of the graph.
Solves only the positive case of a modulus equation or inequality.
Keeps a solution that does not satisfy the original modulus equation.
Sets up the wrong condition for a line to touch, meet or miss a curve.
Applies the functions in the wrong order: works out fg(x) when gf(x) is asked, or the reverse.
Gives 1/f(x) as the inverse, or doesn't swap x and y.
Gives the domain when the range is asked, or writes the range in terms of x instead of f(x).
Includes or excludes an endpoint wrongly, or misses the turning-point value that bounds the range.
States a domain for the inverse that is not the range of the original function.
Uses -m or 1/m instead of -1/m for a perpendicular gradient.
Puts the coordinates into y - y1 = m(x - x1) the wrong way round.
Works out the gradient as change in x over change in y.
Forgets the square root, or adds coordinates instead of subtracting them.
Reads the centre of (x + a)^2 + (y + b)^2 = r^2 with the wrong signs.
Gives r^2 as the radius, or forgets to adjust the constant after completing the square.
Doesn't use the fact that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Gives the distance to the centre when the distance to the circle itself is needed.
Uses a + nd or ar^n where the formula needs n - 1.
Misremembers the arithmetic or geometric sum formula.
Divides an earlier term by a later one to get the common ratio.
Uses a sum to infinity without |r| < 1, or doesn't state the condition when asked.
Solving for n, rounds the wrong way, or leaves a non-integer where a whole number of terms is needed.
Divides by ln r with 0 < r < 1 (a negative number) without reversing the inequality.
Starts a recurrence at the wrong term, or miscounts which term is which.
Counts the terms from r = a to r = b as b - a instead of b - a + 1.
Miscounts the complete periods, or the terms left over, when summing a periodic sequence.
In a sum-formula proof, doesn't write the series both ways round, or skips the adding step.
Doesn't raise the coefficient inside the bracket to the power, e.g. writes (2x)^3 as 2x^3.
Doesn't rewrite (a + bx)^n as a^n(1 + bx/a)^n first, or forgets to raise a to the power n.
Gets nCr wrong, or the product-over-factorial coefficient for a non-integer power.
Loses the alternating signs when expanding (1 - x)^n.
Gives |x| < 1 when the condition is |bx/a| < 1, or rearranges the condition wrongly.
Substitutes an x that doesn't give the target number, or lies outside the range of validity.
Keeps terms beyond the required power, or drops needed ones, when multiplying series.
Uses a false log law, e.g. log(a + b) = log a + log b, or log a / log b = log(a/b).
Brings a power down wrongly, e.g. 2 log x = log 2x, or ln(3^(2x)) = 2 ln(3x).
Takes logs of each term of a sum separately, e.g. from e^x + 1 = y.
Accepts a solution that makes a log argument zero or negative.
Mixes up log base 10 and ln, or changes base wrongly.
Uses t = 1 as the start, or confuses the initial value with a later one.
Uses the wrong sign of k, so a decaying quantity grows.
Mixes up gradient and intercept of the log-linear line, or forgets to undo the log (a = 10^c).
Gives the value of the model when its rate of change (the derivative) is asked.
Uses the wrong time origin or unit, e.g. the calendar year instead of years since the start.
States a limitation that could apply to any model, not one tied to this model or context.
Uses a model well outside the data range without saying the prediction may be unreliable.
Explains a constant in the model without its context or units.
Gets the limiting value as t grows wrong, e.g. forgets that e^(-kt) tends to 0.
Calls the model good or bad without comparing a predicted value with the data.
Works in degrees (or calculator in degree mode) where radians are required, e.g. arc length, calculus, small angles.
Uses r theta or r^2 theta for a sector area, or mixes the arc and area formulas.
Subtracts the wrong triangle area when finding a segment.
Uses the wrong rule, or pairs a side with an angle that is not opposite it.
Misses the obtuse angle that also satisfies the sine rule.
Uses a wrong exact value, e.g. sin 60 degrees = 1/2.
Uses the wrong small-angle form, e.g. cos x ~ 1 - x, or forgets that x must be in radians.
Misremembers a Pythagorean identity, e.g. cos^2 x = 1 + sin^2 x, or sec^2 x = 1 - tan^2 x.
Writes sin 2x as 2 sin x, or picks a form of cos 2x that doesn't help.
Gets the signs wrong in cos(A +/- B) or tan(A +/- B).
Gets R wrong (not sqrt(a^2 + b^2)), inverts tan alpha, or puts alpha in the wrong quadrant or units.
Works on both sides at once, or starts from the identity being proved, without a clear chain.
Confuses sec with 1/sin, or cosec with 1/cos.
Gets the sign of sin or cos wrong for the given quadrant when working from tan.
Gives only the calculator value and misses the other solutions in the interval.
Lists solutions outside the given interval.
Doesn't change the interval for 2x + c before solving sin(2x + c) = k, so solutions are missed.
Keeps an impossible value such as sin x = 2 instead of rejecting it.
Takes the maximum where the trig term is -1 (or the reverse), or gives the wrong time for it.
Gets the sign or the new power wrong when differentiating x^(-n).
Keeps a constant term after differentiating.
Differentiates or integrates 1/x^n or a root term before rewriting it as a power.
Differentiates e^(kx) as e^(kx) (missing k), or ln(kx) as k/x.
Differentiates cos x as sin x, or makes a similar sign error.
In first principles, doesn't expand f(x + h), divide by h, or take the limit (or sets h = 0 too early).
Makes an error when differentiating the first derivative again.
Forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inside function.
Differentiates each factor of a product and multiplies the results.
Swaps the order in the quotient-rule numerator, or forgets to square the denominator.
Leaves the derivative unsimplified when the question asks for a given form.
Doesn't attach dy/dx when differentiating terms in y.
Divides dx/dt by dy/dt instead of dy/dt by dx/dt.
Substitutes an x-coordinate as t without finding the parameter at the point first.
Combines rates the wrong way, e.g. divides where the chain rule multiplies.
Uses the tangent's gradient for the normal, or the reverse.
Uses the derivative expression, still in x, as the gradient of the line.
Uses the wrong y-coordinate for the point, e.g. not found from the curve.
Sets y = 0 instead of dy/dx = 0 to find stationary points.
Finds the x-coordinate of a stationary point but not the y-coordinate.
States maximum or minimum without the second-derivative sign or a gradient check, or without the conclusion.
Concludes a point of inflection just because the second derivative is zero.
Uses the wrong inequality for increasing or decreasing, or the wrong boundary.
Claims a point of inflection without showing the second derivative changes sign.
Differentiates an expression in two variables without eliminating one using the constraint.
Uses a wrong area or volume formula, e.g. misses faces or confuses curved surface area with pi r^2.
Gives the value of x at the optimum when the optimal quantity itself was asked, or the reverse.
Divides by the old power, multiplies instead, or adds 1 wrongly with negative or fractional powers.
Leaves out + c in an indefinite integral.
Doesn't use the given point to find c, or substitutes the wrong coordinate.
Works out F(lower) - F(upper), or makes sign errors substituting a negative limit.
Integrates a product or quotient as a product of integrals instead of expanding or using a method.
Multiplies by k instead of dividing when integrating (ax + b)^n, e^(kx) or 1/(ax + b).
Takes a negative integral as the area, or lets regions above and below the axis cancel.
Subtracts the curves the wrong way round, or integrates between the wrong limits.
Uses limits that are not the intersections or intercepts that bound the region.
Integrates y with respect to t without the dx/dt factor, or uses x-limits for t.
Forgets to add or subtract the triangle or rectangle that makes up part of the region.
Chooses u and dv/dx so that the new integral is harder than the original.
Makes a sign error in uv minus the integral of v du/dx.
Doesn't replace dx with the matching expression in du.
Keeps the x-limits after substituting u, or doesn't substitute back before using them.
Integrates sin^2 x or cos^2 x directly instead of using a double-angle identity.
Integrates sin x as cos x, or makes a similar sign error.
Doesn't combine the log terms into the single ln form the question asks for.
Sets up the wrong form, e.g. misses a term for a repeated factor.
Makes an error finding a constant by substituting values or comparing coefficients.
Tries partial fractions without dividing first, when the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's.
Separates the variables wrongly, e.g. leaves a y term on the x side, or splits by adding.
Turns ln y = f(x) + c into y = e^f(x) + c instead of y = A e^f(x).
Forms a rate equation without a constant of proportionality, or with the wrong sign.
Leaves the solution implicit when the question asks for y in terms of x.
Shows a change of sign but not the continuity condition or the conclusion about the root.
Tests an interval too wide to confirm the accuracy asked, e.g. not a +/- 0.005.
Uses the wrong starting value, or evaluates the iteration wrongly.
Gets f'(x) wrong, or uses x - f'(x)/f(x) instead of x - f(x)/f'(x).
Doesn't say that the method fails because f'(x0) = 0 (the tangent is horizontal).
Doesn't show the algebra that turns the equation into the given iterative form.
Gets the strip width h wrong, e.g. confuses the number of ordinates with the number of strips.
Gets the bracket structure wrong: doubles the end ordinates, or leaves out h/2.
Gives the wrong reason for an over- or under-estimate (it depends on the curve's concavity).
Confuses cobweb and staircase diagrams, or misdescribes whether the iteration converges.
Leaves t in the Cartesian equation, or eliminates it with the wrong identity.
Doesn't give the domain or range of the Cartesian equation that follows from the range of t.
Works out AB as OA - OB instead of OB - OA.
Forgets to square the components or take the square root when finding a magnitude.
Claims vectors are parallel or points collinear without showing a scalar multiple and a common point.
Divides a line in the ratio m:n using m/n instead of m/(m + n).
Assumes the wrong statement at the start of a proof by contradiction.
Checks a few examples instead of giving a general argument.
Finishes the algebra but doesn't write the concluding statement of the proof.
Leaves out a case in a proof by exhaustion.
States a counterexample without showing that it breaks the statement.
Uses the same letter for two different numbers, e.g. 2n and 2n + 1 for 'any two odd numbers'.
Names the wrong sampling method, e.g. calls a quota sample stratified.
Describes a sampling method without its key step, e.g. how units are numbered and chosen at random.
Gives a generic advantage such as 'it is easy' instead of one tied to the method and context.
Confuses the population, the sampling frame and the sample.
Forgets to square the mean in the variance formula, or divides by the wrong n.
Gives the variance when the standard deviation is asked, or the reverse.
Adds the coding constant to the standard deviation, or doesn't scale it.
Finds the wrong position for the median or quartile, or interpolates within the wrong class.
Uses class limits instead of class boundaries, or wrong class widths.
Compares distributions without the context, or without both a location and a spread measure.
Reads bar height as frequency instead of using area (frequency density times width).
Gets the scale factor between area and frequency wrong.
Uses the wrong multiple of the IQR, or the median instead of a quartile, for the outlier limits.
Extends a box-plot whisker to an outlier.
Says one variable causes changes in the other because they are correlated.
Interprets a regression coefficient without context or units, or reads meaning into an intercept outside the data.
Swaps the explanatory and response variables.
Converts back from the log-coded line wrongly, e.g. forgets that b = 10^m.
Multiplies probabilities without independence being given or shown.
Confuses mutually exclusive events with independent ones.
Divides by the wrong probability, e.g. uses P(A and B)/P(A) for P(A|B).
Keeps the second-branch probabilities unchanged when selection is without replacement.
Counts the intersection twice when filling in or adding Venn regions.
Gets 'at least one' wrong, e.g. works out 1 - P(all) instead of 1 - P(none).
Uses the grand total where a row or column total is needed, or the reverse.
Doesn't use the fact that the probabilities sum to 1 to find an unknown.
Uses P(X <= x) where P(X = x) is needed, or the reverse.
Treats P(X < k) as P(X <= k) for a discrete variable, e.g. P(X >= k) = 1 - P(X <= k).
Counts only one order when combining independent outcomes that can happen in several orders.
States the binomial conditions without referring to the context.
Uses the wrong n or p.
Standardises as (mu - x)/sigma, or divides by the variance.
Uses the wrong tail or the wrong sign of z for a given percentage.
Uses a positive z for a value below the mean when setting up simultaneous equations.
Leaves out the continuity correction, or applies it in the wrong direction.
Uses np as the variance, or the wrong standard deviation, in the normal approximation.
Models the situation with an unsuitable distribution for the conditions given.
Writes the hypotheses in words, or without the parameter (p, rho or mu).
Picks a one-tailed test when the claim is two-tailed, or the reverse, or the wrong direction.
Doesn't show the probabilities on either side of the critical value.
Takes the critical region one value too far, so its probability exceeds the significance level.
Uses the full significance level in each tail of a two-tailed test.
Compares P(X = x) with the significance level instead of the tail probability.
Says the test 'proves' something, or concludes without the context.
Uses sigma instead of sigma/sqrt(n) for the distribution of the sample mean.
Reads the PMCC critical value for the wrong sample size or tail.
Gives the nominal significance level when the actual probability of the critical region is asked.
Changes which direction is positive partway through, e.g. g positive both up and down.
Takes u = 0 when the particle is not starting from rest.
Doesn't convert to SI units, e.g. leaves km/h or grams.
Uses the area under a velocity-time graph for acceleration, or its gradient for distance.
Gives displacement when total distance is asked, or the reverse, when the particle changes direction.
Gives a velocity vector or one component when the speed (a magnitude) is asked.
Measures the direction from the wrong axis or reference line.
Uses constant-acceleration formulas when the acceleration varies with time.
Doesn't use the initial position or velocity to find the constant of integration.
Uses sin for the horizontal and cos for the vertical component (or the reverse) against the diagram.
Includes acceleration due to gravity in the horizontal motion.
Uses different times for the horizontal and vertical motion of the same flight.
Sets the whole velocity to zero at the top instead of just the vertical component.
Leaves out a force such as the normal reaction, friction or tension.
Uses sin where cos is needed when resolving, or the reverse.
Uses m instead of mg for the weight.
Doesn't set resultant force equal to ma: treats ma as an extra force, or gets the direction wrong.
Includes internal tension in the whole-system equation, or uses different tensions for a light inextensible string.
Uses mg rather than mg sin(theta) along the slope, or swaps the components.
Gives a final answer to more significant figures than the value of g used justifies.
Uses mu times mg for friction when the normal reaction is not mg, e.g. on a slope or with an angled pull.
Points friction the wrong way, not opposing the motion or the likely motion.
Uses F = mu R when the friction is not at its limit.
Decides whether an object moves without comparing the driving force with the maximum friction.
Uses the distance along the rod instead of the perpendicular distance, or forgets the sin(theta).
Leaves out the moment of one force, or gives a moment to a force acting through the pivot.
Mixes clockwise and anticlockwise moments in the same equation.
Draws the reaction at a smooth contact in the wrong direction, i.e. not perpendicular to the surface.
Puts the weight at the wrong point, e.g. at the midpoint of a non-uniform rod.
Gives a modelling assumption that doesn't affect this problem, e.g. air resistance in a statics question.
Names an assumption or refinement without saying how it changes the answer.
